name: Prime and composite numbers
summary: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors. A composite has more than two.
mental: Try dividing by primes no greater than the square root; any larger factor must have a smaller partner.
example: For 29, test 2, 3 and 5. None divides it, so 29 is prime.
misconception: 1 is neither prime nor composite.
interview: Explain prime and composite numbers in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors. A composite has more than two. Try dividing by primes no greater than the square root; any larger factor must have a smaller partner.

reviewer: Technical reference check; no external peer review

activity.title: Prime and composite numbers · Check your understanding

activity.solution: 29 has no prime factor at or below √29. The others are 1 or products.

name: Successive percentage change
summary: A percentage is a proportion of a stated base. Successive changes multiply their growth factors.
mental: Track the base after each change rather than adding percentages.
example: 100 × 1.2 × 0.8 = 96. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall loses 4%.
misconception: Equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel.
interview: Explain successive percentage change in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: A percentage is a proportion of a stated base. Successive changes multiply their growth factors. Track the base after each change rather than adding percentages.

name: Dividing in a ratio
summary: A ratio describes relative amounts; it does not specify the total.
mental: Add the parts, find one part, then scale.
example: Split 600 in the ratio 2:3: five parts mean 120 per part; the shares are 240 and 360.
misconception: The first share of a 2:3 split is 2/5, not 2/3, of the total.
interview: Explain dividing in a ratio in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: A ratio describes relative amounts; it does not specify the total. Add the parts, find one part, then scale.

name: Combined work rates
summary: Work rates add when workers independently contribute to the same task.
mental: Use a common job unit per day. Add fractions of a job, not completion times.
example: A needs 6 days and B needs 3. Their daily rates are 1/6 and 1/3; together 1/2, so they need 2 days.
misconception: Adding completion times gives the wrong unit and result.
interview: Explain combined work rates in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: Work rates add when workers independently contribute to the same task. Use a common job unit per day. Add fractions of a job, not completion times.

name: Average speed
summary: Average speed is total distance divided by total elapsed time.
mental: First add distances and times, then divide. Equal distances and equal times behave differently.
example: Travel 60 km at 30 km/h and 60 km at 60 km/h: 120 km in 3 hours gives 40 km/h.
misconception: The arithmetic mean of speeds works for equal durations, not equal distances.
interview: Explain average speed in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: Average speed is total distance divided by total elapsed time. First add distances and times, then divide. Equal distances and equal times behave differently.

activity.solution: For equal distances the average is 2ab/(a+b) = 4800/100 = 48.

name: Java values and references
summary: Java passes argument values. For an object variable, that value is a reference to an object.
mental: Copying a reference lets two variables reach one object. Reassigning one local variable does not reassign the caller’s variable.
example: A method can mutate a supplied list, but assigning its parameter to a new list does not replace the caller’s list.
misconception: Java does not pass caller variables by reference.
interview: Explain java values and references in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: Java passes argument values. For an object variable, that value is a reference to an object. Copying a reference lets two variables reach one object. Reassigning one local variable does not reassign the caller’s variable.

activity.solution: Only the copied reference value in the parameter was reassigned.

misconception: A HashMap has no promised encounter order.

name: SELECT and NULL
summary: SELECT constructs a result from relations. NULL represents an unknown or absent value; comparisons with it are not ordinary Boolean equality.
mental: Think in rows and predicates. WHERE keeps rows whose predicate is true.
example: SELECT name FROM people WHERE manager_id IS NULL returns people with no known manager.
misconception: Use IS NULL, not = NULL.
interview: Explain select and null in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: SELECT constructs a result from relations. NULL represents an unknown or absent value; comparisons with it are not ordinary Boolean equality. Think in rows and predicates. WHERE keeps rows whose predicate is true.

name: LEFT JOIN and missing matches
summary: A LEFT JOIN retains every left row, adding matching right values or NULLs when no match exists.
mental: Separate the matching condition in ON from filtering the joined result in WHERE.
example: Customers LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id retains customers with no orders.
misconception: A right-side WHERE predicate can discard unmatched rows and change the intended outer-join behavior.
interview: Explain left join and missing matches in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: A LEFT JOIN retains every left row, adding matching right values or NULLs when no match exists. Separate the matching condition in ON from filtering the joined result in WHERE.

name: GROUP BY and HAVING
summary: Grouping collects rows sharing a key; aggregate functions summarize each group. HAVING filters groups.
mental: WHERE applies before grouping, HAVING after aggregation.
example: SELECT team, COUNT(*) FROM members GROUP BY team HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 finds teams with at least three members.
misconception: COUNT(column) skips NULL values; COUNT(*) counts rows.
interview: Explain group by and having in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: Grouping collects rows sharing a key; aggregate functions summarize each group. HAVING filters groups. WHERE applies before grouping, HAVING after aggregation.

name: Functional dependencies and 3NF
summary: A functional dependency X → Y means equal X values determine equal Y values. Normalization reduces dependency-driven redundancy.
mental: Put facts with the key that determines them, while checking lossless decomposition and dependency preservation.
example: If employee_id determines department_id and department_id determines department_name, storing department_name per employee repeats a department fact.
misconception: More tables do not automatically imply better normalization or faster queries.
interview: Explain functional dependencies and 3nf in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: A functional dependency X → Y means equal X values determine equal Y values. Normalization reduces dependency-driven redundancy. Put facts with the key that determines them, while checking lossless decomposition and dependency preservation.

name: Lost updates and isolation
summary: Concurrent transactions can overwrite each other’s read-modify-write work. Isolation controls permitted observations and interleavings.
mental: Write down both transactions in time order. Ask what each read and which changes survived.
example: Both read 100. A writes 80, then B writes 70 based on its stale 100. A’s debit can be lost.
misconception: The exact anomalies prevented at each isolation level depend on the database engine.
interview: Explain lost updates and isolation in your own words, then give a concrete example and one limitation.
interviewAnswer: Concurrent transactions can overwrite each other’s read-modify-write work. Isolation controls permitted observations and interleavings. Write down both transactions in time order. Ask what each read and which changes survived.

name: Mutex and critical sections
summary: A critical section accesses shared state that must satisfy an invariant. A mutex can serialize that section.
mental: Protect the whole invariant, including every related read and write.
